rawEventDetails: Details Event Description Joint CEE/MAE Distinguished Seminar Abstract: This talk will discuss two peculiar effects we recently discovered: the photomolecular effect and the evaporative refrigeration effect. To explain super-thermal solar-interfacial evaporation from hydrogels and other porous materials, we hypothesize that photons can directly cleave off water clusters at the liquid-vapor interface in a way similar to the photoelectric effect, which we call the photomolecular effect. I will discuss experimental evidence we have so far. This photomolecular evaporation process may exist widely in nature. Our studies on photomolecular evaporation also led us to investigate peculiarities in thermal evaporation. At an evaporating interface, a temperature discontinuity exists between the liquid and the vapor sides, which was predicted by theories and observed in some experiments. However, the existing theories cannot explain experiments. We develop a new interfacial condition that can be used to couple transport on both sides of the interface, leading to agreements between theory and experiments. Our modeling reveals the existence of a new refrigeration effect: the vapor temperature can drop below that of the liquid film and in fact, lower than even the condensing surface temperature. This effect has yet to be confirmed experimentally and may find applications in air-conditioning and refrigeration. Biography: Gang Chen is the Carl Richard Soderberg Professor of Power Engineering at Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT). He served as the Department Head of the Department of Mechanical Engineering at MIT from 2013 to 2018. He obtained his PhD degree from the Mechanical Engineering Department at UC Berkeley under the supervision of then UC Berkeley Chancellor Chang-Lin Tien. He was a faculty member at Duke University and UCLA, before joining MIT in 2001. He received an NSF Young Investigator Award, an R&D 100 award, an ASME Heat Transfer Memorial Award, an ASME Frank Kreith Award in Energy, a Nukiyama Memorial Award by the Japan Heat Transfer Society, a World Technology Network Award in Energy, an Eringen medal from the Society of Engineering Science, the Capers and Marion McDonald Award for Excellences in Mentoring and Advising from MIT, a Steven Chu medal from the Asian American Academy of Science and Engineering, and an American Courage Award from Asian American Advancing Justice. He serves on the board of the Asian American Scholar Forum. He is a fellow of the American Association for the Advancement of Science, the American Physical Society, The American Society of Mechanical Engineers, and the Guggenheim Foundation. He is a foreign member of the Chinese Academy of Sciences, an academician of Academy Sinica, a fellow of the American Academy of Arts and Sciences, and a member of the US National Academy of Engineering and a member of the US National Academy of Science.

rawEventDetails: Details Event Description Abstract Complex systems can fail in many ways, from cascading failures triggered by random component loss to deliberately targeted attacks. This raises a fundamental question: How can robustness be quantified when a disturbance changes the probability distribution of system outcomes? This talk develops a probabilistic perspective on robustness in which changes in system performance are represented through changes in outcome distributions. Drawing on information theory, these changes are quantified through an entropy-based robustness index that compares system behaviour before and after a disturbance. The index builds on concepts and methods from system reliability and complements conventional reliability and risk measures by characterizing how system behaviour changes when disrupted. About the Speaker Alex Sixie Cao is an Assistant Professor in the School of Civil and Environmental Engineering at Nanyang Technological University, Singapore, where he leads the Risk and Infrastructure Systems Lab. His work spans impact loading and structural mechanics, mechanical and probabilistic modelling of progressive collapse and cascading failures, quantitative measures of robustness, and risk-informed decision-making. Alex also studies how structural safety objectives and infrastructure decisions should evolve under long-term environmental and societal change, including climate change. He received his doctorate from ETH Zurich, where his research focused on modelling progressive collapse in buildings, and his MSc in Structural Engineering from the Norwegian University of Science and Technology. Before joining NTU, he was a postdoctoral researcher at Empa and ETH Zurich, working across structural mechanics, system reliability, and robustness. rawEventDetails: Details Event Description Alessandro Vespignani, Professor of Physics, Northeastern University, opens the CCS Distinguished Seminar Series. The talk is free and open to the University community. Abstract Concepts developed to describe spreading processes on networks, including the role of heterogeneous connectivity, have provided the foundation for a new generation of mechanistic models. Built on empirical mobility and contact networks, these models capture the multi-scale nature of contagion in real populations. These methodological and data integration advances enabled epidemic modeling to evolve into a public-service activity, generating forecasts and analytics that inform policy in real time. The same framework supports the design of surveillance systems, such as global aircraft-based wastewater monitoring, where the structure of the air-transportation network becomes an asset for early detection. The lecture will discuss this trajectory and why consolidating these capabilities is now a central requirement of pandemic preparedness beyond emergency response. About the speaker Alessandro Vespignani is the Sternberg Family Distinguished University Professor at Northeastern University, where he founded and directs the Network Science Institute. His research focuses on the modeling of contagion processes in complex networks, from the spread of infectious diseases to the diffusion of information. He leads EPISTORM, a national center for epidemic emergency analytics funded by the U.S. CDC. He is elected Fellow of the APS, the Network Science Society, and the AAAS. His awards include the Euler Award and the EPS Statistical and Nonlinear Physics Prize.
